script.opening: (Tense, arms crossed, speaks fast.) "The nurse said she'd noticed something during my smear and asked me to see you … about the cutting I had as a little girl, back home. Am I in trouble? Are you going to report me to the police? I didn't choose it — it was done to me when I was 6. Please don't make this a big thing."

facts.text: Cut at age 6 in Sierra Leone, at her grandmother's village; came to the UK at 14. Doesn't know what "type" — "they took away a lot." Smear last week was difficult and painful.
If asked gently: periods are painful and slow to come out; takes a long time to pass urine; urine infections two or three times a year; sex has always been painful. No current discharge or infection.
Not pregnant; on the implant. Hopes to have children "one day" with her partner. "Would it be a problem?" — didn't know about deinfibulation: "I didn't know that was possible."

When asked: "Why do you need to know? I'd never let anyone do that to a child." If the reason is explained: no children of her own. Her sister (lives locally) has a 5-year-old daughter; their mother visits Sierra Leone often. "I'd need to think about who you mean. I don't want anyone getting into trouble."
"I've never really talked about any of that with anyone." Has flashbacks before smears and intimate examinations. "I don't like thinking about it." No thoughts of self-harm.
Healthcare assistant in a care home. Lives with her partner, Ibrahim, who knows. No medicines except the implant, no allergies.

Frightened of the police and of being judged. Visible relief if the doctor clearly says she is not in trouble: "(Exhales.) Okay. I was so scared." Asks: "So the police won't see it?" and "What's the second thing?" Becomes guarded when asked about girls in the family; engages if the doctor explains it's about protecting children, not blaming her. If the doctor says the police will be told, become distressed and want to end the call.

ice.ideas: "Because they found it, I'll be reported to the police."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of police and of her family getting into trouble; shame and being looked at differently; she has never spoken about the trauma.
ice.expectations: "To be told I'm not in trouble — and not to make it a big thing."

cues: "Am I in trouble?" — needs clear reassurance first.
"I don't want anyone getting into trouble." — when the family is raised.
"I've never really talked about any of that." — opening for support.

checkpoints.text: Responds with TRAUMA-INFORMED, non-judgemental care — reassures she is a survivor, not in trouble, and treats her with dignity and cultural sensitivity

Corrects the police fear accurately: an ADULT with historical FGM is NOT reported to police; the statutory mandatory-reporting duty applies to KNOWN FGM in a girl UNDER 18, not a woman aged 18 or over (her FGM was done to her at 6)
Knows the duties that DO apply — RECORD the FGM in the record and the FGM Enhanced Dataset (mandatory; no consent needed, but she is told) — and explains that recording ≠ reporting to police

Carries out a SAFEGUARDING RISK ASSESSMENT for any girls at risk (daughters, sisters, nieces) and would make a safeguarding referral if a child is at risk, flagging any daughter under 18 on FGM-IS — the key safeguarding action
Assesses and addresses HER clinical/psychological needs (type/complications, deinfibulation especially for type 3, psychological impact) and refers to specialist FGM services
Immediately reassures about the police fear, explains what actually happens clearly, and avoids retraumatising or alienating her
Holds the cultural and trauma context with compassion while remaining clear FGM is harmful/illegal, framing identification as a route to help

Safety-nets and follows up: records appropriately, completes the risk assessment/referral for at-risk girls, refers her to FGM/psychological services, and arranges follow-up — correct duties discharged compassionately

worked.txt: "Let me put your mind at rest straight away: you are not in trouble, and I am not reporting you to the police. This was done to you as a little girl — you’re the person it was done to, not someone who did anything wrong."

"There are a couple of things I do need to do, and I’ll be open about them. I note it in your records, and GP practices have to add it to a national NHS FGM dataset — I don’t need your permission for that, but I want you to know, and the published figures don’t name anyone. That’s just recording, not a police report. They’re completely different things."

"The thing we DO have to think about is protecting any young girls in your family from this. Do you have daughters, or younger sisters or nieces? … If any girl could be at risk, that’s where we’d step in to protect them — it’s not about you. If you have a daughter, her health record can carry a note so any nurse or doctor who sees her knows the family history."

"More importantly, this is a chance to help YOU. Are you having any problems — with your waterworks, periods, pain or discomfort? There’s a procedure that can help with some types, and specialist clinics that support women who’ve been through this — they’d examine you properly in person."
"And it can leave a real emotional mark. If you’d find it helpful, I can arrange support to talk things through — no pressure, it’s there if you want it."

"You’ve done nothing wrong by coming today, and I’m glad we can support you. I’ll refer you to the specialist service, and you can come back to me anytime. Is there anything you’re still worried about?"

f.learning: FGM identified in an ADULT during a smear is, first and foremost, a moment for trauma-informed, non-judgemental survivor care: she underwent childhood abuse, is anxious and possibly ashamed, and must be reassured immediately that she is not in trouble and not being reported to the police — mishandling this, or threatening police, would retraumatise her and destroy trust. The reporting position must be understood correctly: there is NO duty to report an adult with historical FGM to the police (she has committed no offence), because the statutory MANDATORY police-reporting duty applies specifically to KNOWN/identified FGM in a girl UNDER 18, not to a woman aged 18 or over whose FGM was done to her as a child. There ARE duties, however: you must RECORD the finding in her medical record and the FGM Enhanced Dataset (mandatory for GP practices; her consent is not required, but she is told; a clinical/data duty distinct from a criminal report — recording is not reporting to police), and — the critical safeguarding action — carry out a RISK ASSESSMENT for any girls connected to her (daughters, younger sisters, nieces) who could be at risk of FGM, making a safeguarding referral if a child is at risk and flagging any daughter under 18 on the FGM Information Sharing system (FGM-IS). Assess and address her clinical needs (the type of FGM and its complications — urinary, menstrual, sexual, obstetric — and the option of deinfibulation, especially for type 3 and ideally before pregnancy/delivery) and her psychological needs (flashbacks, anxiety, sexual difficulties), referring to specialist FGM services (RCOG GTG 53) and offering psychological support (NICE NG116), because the point of identifying it is to help her. The hidden agenda is fear of being reported, judged, or having "a big thing" made of it, with shame and trauma beneath; discharge the duties correctly and compassionately, reassure about the police fear, explain clearly what actually happens, protect any at-risk girls, and treat her with dignity.

knowledge.guideline: FGM Act 2003 (as amended by the Serious Crime Act 2015) · Mandatory reporting of FGM: procedural information (Home Office/DH) · FGM Enhanced Dataset (NHS England) · FGM risk and safeguarding guidance for professionals (DH) · RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 53 (2015) · NICE NG116
knowledge.summary: An adult with FGM done in childhood is a survivor, not an offender. She is not reported to the police; her FGM is recorded, girls in her family are risk-assessed, and she is offered care.

points.h: No police report for an adult
points.t: The mandatory reporting duty applies only when a girl under 18 discloses FGM or physical signs are seen in a girl under 18. It does not apply to women aged 18 and over, or to girls at risk (Home Office procedural information).

Recording FGM is mandatory for GP practices, acute trusts and mental health trusts. Record it in her notes and submit to the FGM Enhanced Dataset each time FGM is identified or treated. Her consent is not required, but explain the dataset to her; published data are anonymous.

When an adult woman is found to have FGM, ask whether she has daughters or other girls under 18 in her family and assess their risk (DH risk and safeguarding guidance; RCOG GTG 53). A girl under 18 with a family history of FGM can be flagged on the national FGM Information Sharing system (FGM-IS). Refer to children’s social care if any girl is at risk.
WHO classification (international): type 1 clitoridectomy, type 2 excision, type 3 infibulation (narrowing of the vaginal opening with a covering seal), type 4 other harmful procedures.

Ask about urinary symptoms and infections, painful or prolonged periods, pain with sex and future pregnancy. RCOG GTG 53: offer referral to a specialist FGM service; deinfibulation can be offered for type 3, ideally before pregnancy or antenatally.
Ask about flashbacks, avoidance and low mood. NICE NG116: offer trauma-focused psychological therapy for clinically important PTSD symptoms.

dg.d: Checked privacy; responded first to her question about the police before any agenda.
Explored her fears about family and being judged, and her feelings around examinations.
Offered specialist FGM clinic examination; planned a trauma-informed approach to future screening; no examination forced.
Type of FGM unknown; urinary, menstrual, sexual and obstetric complications; psychological trauma; girls at risk.
Screened for urinary retention, infection and PTSD symptoms; considered risk to any girls under 18.
Adult survivor of childhood FGM: not a police matter; recording and safeguarding assessment apply.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Record and Enhanced Dataset explained; FGM-IS for daughters; specialist FGM referral; deinfibulation discussed; psychological therapy offered.
Psychological impact and future pregnancy planning addressed.
Review in two weeks to complete the risk assessment; urgent symptoms and at-risk girls safety-net.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “please don’t make this a big thing” and “I don’t like thinking about it” and responded.
Idea (she will be reported), concern (family in trouble, being judged), expectation (reassurance, not a big deal).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear of police and of her family getting into trouble; shame and being looked at differently; she has never spoken about the trauma — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, Ms Conteh, I’m Dr Okafor. Thank you for coming back to talk to me. Are you somewhere private? Tell me how you’re feeling about today.
model.why: Checks privacy and opens with her feelings

model.text: The nurse said she’d noticed something during my smear, about the cutting I had as a little girl back home. Am I in trouble? Are you going to report me to the police? I didn’t choose it — it was done to me when I was 6. Please don’t make this a big thing.
Let me answer that straight away: you are not in trouble, and I am not reporting you to the police. This was done to you as a child. You haven’t done anything wrong.
model.why: Corrects the police fear immediately and accurately

model.text: (Exhales.) Okay. I was so scared.
I’m sorry you’ve been frightened. I’d like to explain what happens now, check how you are in yourself, and see whether there’s anything we can help with. Is that all right?
Yes.

I want to be open with you about two things. First, I write it in your medical record, as we do for every woman who has had FGM, and some of that information goes to an NHS dataset. The published figures never name anyone. That is recording, not reporting to the police — they’re completely different.
model.why: Explains the recording duty and the Enhanced Dataset honestly

model.text: So the police won’t see it?
No. The law only asks us to tell the police when a girl under 18 has had FGM. You’re an adult, so that doesn’t apply to you.
model.why: States the scope of mandatory reporting correctly

model.text: What’s the second thing?

The second is about protecting girls. Because it happened in your family, we ask every woman in your situation whether there are daughters, sisters or nieces under 18 who might be at risk. It’s not about blaming you. Is that something you’d be willing to talk about?
model.why: Introduces the safeguarding risk assessment for girls

model.text: Why do you need to know? I’d never let anyone do that to a child.

I believe you, and I can hear how strongly you feel. We ask everyone, because sometimes it’s other relatives who decide. If you have a daughter, we would note the family history in her record so that the people caring for her know to support you in protecting her.
I’d need to think about who you mean. I don’t want anyone getting into trouble.
That’s fair. Let’s come back to it before we finish. If any girl were at risk, I would share that with children’s social care to protect her — and I’d tell you first.
model.why: Is honest about when a referral would follow

model.text: Now, this is also a chance to help you. Some women have problems they’ve never mentioned: trouble passing urine, infections, painful or heavy periods, or pain during sex. Do any of those happen to you?
I’ve never really talked about any of that with anyone.

Thank you for telling me — you can talk about as much or as little as you like. Is pregnancy something you’re thinking about, now or in the future? Some types of cutting need planning ahead of pregnancy and birth.
Would it be a problem?

It depends on the type. Where the opening has been narrowed, there’s a small operation called deinfibulation that opens it, which can make periods, passing urine, sex and birth easier. It’s best done before a pregnancy. A specialist FGM clinic, where the staff see this every day, can examine you and talk it through.
I didn’t know that was possible.
And how has it affected you emotionally? Some women get memories coming back, nightmares, or feel anxious around smears or being examined.
I don’t like thinking about it.
That makes a lot of sense. Before today, what did you think would happen?
model.why: Explores her original ideas and concerns

model.text: That I’d be reported and my family would be in trouble. That people would look at me differently.
I’m glad we’ve cleared that up. What would be most helpful for you now?
Maybe the clinic. I want to understand what my options are.

Then let’s do this: I’ll refer you to the specialist FGM clinic. For your next smear, we can book a longer appointment with a nurse you know, and you can stop at any time. If you’d like, I can also refer you for talking therapy — that’s your choice.
model.why: Shared plan with specialist, trauma-informed screening and psychological support

model.text: The clinic yes. The talking I’ll think about.
That’s completely fine. And about girls in your family — would you be willing to come back and talk that through, or do it now?
model.why: Returns to the risk assessment rather than dropping it

model.text: I’ll come back. I understand why you ask.

Thank you. If you have fever, severe pain, or can’t pass urine, get seen the same day. And if you ever hear of a girl who might be taken to be cut, tell me or call the police straight away. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
No police for me. You record it. I go to the FGM clinic, we talk about the girls in my family next time, and I call if anything is urgent.
That’s right. I’ll book you back in two weeks. You’ve done nothing wrong by coming today.
model.why: Defined follow-up and closes with dignity

social.t: Fear of her family being blamed may stop her engaging. Keep the focus on her care and on protecting girls, not on blame.
If an interpreter is needed, use a professional one, not a relative or community member.

legal.t: FGM Act 2003 section 5B (added 2015): applies only to girls under 18 who disclose FGM or have physical signs of it. Not to adults.
FGM Enhanced Dataset: mandatory submission by GP practices each time FGM is identified or treated; no consent needed, but explain it.
Refer to children’s social care under local safeguarding procedures; FGM Protection Orders can prevent travel if a girl is at risk abroad.

professional.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain, offer a chaperone and get consent; she can stop an examination at any time.
Tell her what you will record and when you would share information, before she tells you anything about girls in her family.

community.t: NHS specialist FGM clinics (including self-referral in many areas) and FGM survivor support organisations.

redFlags: Urinary retention, fever or severe pelvic pain — same-day assessment
Pregnancy with type 3 FGM — urgent specialist antenatal referral
A girl under 18 at risk or already cut — safeguarding referral or mandatory police report
Suicidal thoughts or severe PTSD symptoms
psychosocial: Fear of the police and of family being blamed
Emotional impact, flashbacks and fear of examination
ice: Idea: “Being found with FGM means I’ll be reported”
Concern: her family getting into trouble; being judged
Expectation: reassurance and for it not to become “a big thing”

playbook.diagnosis: “The nurse saw signs of the cutting that was done to you as a child. You’re not in trouble. I need to record it, think about any girls in the family, and offer you help.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Writing it in your notes is like writing down an operation you had as a child — it helps the people who care for you. It isn’t a police report.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in scared you’d be reported. You won’t be. What we can do is help with anything it has left you with.”
management.psychosocial: Go at her pace, make future smears gentler, and offer talking therapy without pressure.
sharedPlan: Record in notes and submit to the FGM Enhanced Dataset, explained to her
Risk assessment for any girls under 18; FGM-IS flag for daughters; referral if at risk
Specialist FGM clinic referral, including deinfibulation discussion; psychological therapy offered
safetyNet: Urinary retention, fever or severe pain — same day
Review in two weeks to complete the risk conversation

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you know which duty applies to whom. Candidates fail by threatening the police, by skipping the question about girls, or by forgetting that she is a patient with needs of her own.

items.fail: Telling her FGM must be reported to the police.
items.why: The mandatory duty applies to girls under 18 only. Getting this wrong frightens a survivor and is factually incorrect.
items.fix: “You’re not being reported. That law is about girls under 18.”

items.fail: Not recording it, because she asked you not to make it a big thing.
items.why: Recording and the Enhanced Dataset submission are mandatory for GP practices.
items.fix: Explain that recording is not reporting, and that published figures don’t name anyone.

items.fail: Never asking about daughters or other girls in the family.
items.why: The safeguarding focus is on girls at risk. This is the key action examiners look for.
items.fix: Ask routinely, explain FGM-IS, and be honest about when you would refer.

items.fail: Interrogating her about the girls in a way that feels like blame.
items.why: She will close down, and the risk goes unassessed.
items.fix: Normalise it: “We ask every woman who has been through this.”

items.fail: Ignoring urinary, menstrual, sexual, obstetric and emotional effects.
items.why: Identifying FGM is meant to lead to care. Missing deinfibulation before pregnancy is a clinical gap.
items.fix: Ask about each and refer to a specialist FGM clinic.

items.fail: Dropping the risk question when she says she needs to think.
items.why: An unfinished safeguarding assessment is unsafe.
items.fix: Agree a date to return to it and document the plan.

timeMap.d: She asks if she will be reported. Say no, clearly, in the first minute.
Recording and the dataset (not reporting); mandatory reporting is for under-18s only.
Urinary, periods, sex, pregnancy plans, emotional impact. Deinfibulation and specialist clinic.
Her fears about family and judgement; what she wants now.
FGM clinic, talking therapy offer, gentler smears; return to the girls-at-risk question; safety-net; review.

wordPics.fail: Tells her the police must be informed, or says nothing is needed and does not record it; never asks about girls in the family; ignores her health needs; interrogates or judges her.
wordPics.pass: Reassures her she is not reported; mentions recording; asks about daughters; offers a specialist referral; is kind and non-judgemental.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the difference between recording and reporting in plain words; explains FGM-IS and when a referral would follow; asks about urinary, menstrual, sexual, obstetric and psychological effects; explains deinfibulation; offers a trauma-informed plan for future screening; returns to the risk question rather than dropping it; uses teach-back.

avoid.dont: "I have a legal duty to report FGM to the police."
avoid.instead: "You’re not in trouble and I’m not reporting you. That law is about girls under 18."
avoid.why: Wrong for an adult, and it would retraumatise her and destroy trust.

avoid.dont: "Do your daughters live with you? Have they been cut?"
avoid.instead: "We ask every woman who has been through this whether there are girls in the family we can help protect."
avoid.why: An accusatory question feels like an interrogation; a routine framing gets an honest answer.

avoid.dont: "It’s all in the past, so there’s nothing to do."
avoid.instead: "This is a chance to help you — some women have problems they’ve never mentioned."
avoid.why: It misses her health needs and the recording and safeguarding duties.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An adult with FGM done in childhood is a survivor, not an offender. She is not reported to the police; her FGM is recorded, girls in her family are risk-assessed, and she is offered care.

points.h: No police report for an adult
points.t: The mandatory reporting duty applies only when a girl under 18 discloses FGM or physical signs are seen in a girl under 18. It does not apply to women aged 18 and over, or to girls at risk (Home Office procedural information).

Recording FGM is mandatory for GP practices, acute trusts and mental health trusts. Record it in her notes and submit to the FGM Enhanced Dataset each time FGM is identified or treated. Her consent is not required, but explain the dataset to her; published data are anonymous.

When an adult woman is found to have FGM, ask whether she has daughters or other girls under 18 in her family and assess their risk (DH risk and safeguarding guidance; RCOG GTG 53). A girl under 18 with a family history of FGM can be flagged on the national FGM Information Sharing system (FGM-IS). Refer to children’s social care if any girl is at risk.
WHO classification (international): type 1 clitoridectomy, type 2 excision, type 3 infibulation (narrowing of the vaginal opening with a covering seal), type 4 other harmful procedures.

Ask about urinary symptoms and infections, painful or prolonged periods, pain with sex and future pregnancy. RCOG GTG 53: offer referral to a specialist FGM service; deinfibulation can be offered for type 3, ideally before pregnancy or antenatally.
Ask about flashbacks, avoidance and low mood. NICE NG116: offer trauma-focused psychological therapy for clinically important PTSD symptoms.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy; responded first to her question about the police before any agenda.
Explored her fears about family and being judged, and her feelings around examinations.
Picked up “please don’t make this a big thing” and “I don’t like thinking about it” and responded.
Idea (she will be reported), concern (family in trouble, being judged), expectation (reassurance, not a big deal).
Offered specialist FGM clinic examination; planned a trauma-informed approach to future screening; no examination forced.
Type of FGM unknown; urinary, menstrual, sexual and obstetric complications; psychological trauma; girls at risk.
Screened for urinary retention, infection and PTSD symptoms; considered risk to any girls under 18.
Adult survivor of childhood FGM: not a police matter; recording and safeguarding assessment apply.
Record and Enhanced Dataset explained; FGM-IS for daughters; specialist FGM referral; deinfibulation discussed; psychological therapy offered.
Psychological impact and future pregnancy planning addressed.
Review in two weeks to complete the risk assessment; urgent symptoms and at-risk girls safety-net.

social.t: Fear of her family being blamed may stop her engaging. Keep the focus on her care and on protecting girls, not on blame.
If an interpreter is needed, use a professional one, not a relative or community member.

legal.t: FGM Act 2003 section 5B (added 2015): applies only to girls under 18 who disclose FGM or have physical signs of it. Not to adults.
FGM Enhanced Dataset: mandatory submission by GP practices each time FGM is identified or treated; no consent needed, but explain it.
Refer to children’s social care under local safeguarding procedures; FGM Protection Orders can prevent travel if a girl is at risk abroad.

professional.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain, offer a chaperone and get consent; she can stop an examination at any time.
Tell her what you will record and when you would share information, before she tells you anything about girls in her family.

community.t: NHS specialist FGM clinics (including self-referral in many areas) and FGM survivor support organisations.

redFlags: Urinary retention, fever or severe pelvic pain — same-day assessment
Pregnancy with type 3 FGM — urgent specialist antenatal referral
A girl under 18 at risk or already cut — safeguarding referral or mandatory police report
Suicidal thoughts or severe PTSD symptoms
psychosocial: Fear of the police and of family being blamed
Emotional impact, flashbacks and fear of examination
ice: Idea: “Being found with FGM means I’ll be reported”
Concern: her family getting into trouble; being judged
Expectation: reassurance and for it not to become “a big thing”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The nurse saw signs of the cutting that was done to you as a child. You’re not in trouble. I need to record it, think about any girls in the family, and offer you help.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Writing it in your notes is like writing down an operation you had as a child — it helps the people who care for you. It isn’t a police report.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in scared you’d be reported. You won’t be. What we can do is help with anything it has left you with.”
management.psychosocial: Go at her pace, make future smears gentler, and offer talking therapy without pressure.
sharedPlan: Record in notes and submit to the FGM Enhanced Dataset, explained to her
Risk assessment for any girls under 18; FGM-IS flag for daughters; referral if at risk
Specialist FGM clinic referral, including deinfibulation discussion; psychological therapy offered
safetyNet: Urinary retention, fever or severe pain — same day
Review in two weeks to complete the risk conversation

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you know which duty applies to whom. Candidates fail by threatening the police, by skipping the question about girls, or by forgetting that she is a patient with needs of her own.

items.fail: Telling her FGM must be reported to the police.
items.why: The mandatory duty applies to girls under 18 only. Getting this wrong frightens a survivor and is factually incorrect.
items.fix: “You’re not being reported. That law is about girls under 18.”

items.fail: Not recording it, because she asked you not to make it a big thing.
items.why: Recording and the Enhanced Dataset submission are mandatory for GP practices.
items.fix: Explain that recording is not reporting, and that published figures don’t name anyone.

items.fail: Never asking about daughters or other girls in the family.
items.why: The safeguarding focus is on girls at risk. This is the key action examiners look for.
items.fix: Ask routinely, explain FGM-IS, and be honest about when you would refer.

items.fail: Interrogating her about the girls in a way that feels like blame.
items.why: She will close down, and the risk goes unassessed.
items.fix: Normalise it: “We ask every woman who has been through this.”

items.fail: Ignoring urinary, menstrual, sexual, obstetric and emotional effects.
items.why: Identifying FGM is meant to lead to care. Missing deinfibulation before pregnancy is a clinical gap.
items.fix: Ask about each and refer to a specialist FGM clinic.

items.fail: Dropping the risk question when she says she needs to think.
items.why: An unfinished safeguarding assessment is unsafe.
items.fix: Agree a date to return to it and document the plan.
